source.title: Trends in Invasive Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Infections

extraction_metadata.schema_note: For descriptive quantitative epidemiology, the current LiteratureAtom schema requires exposures. Age, epidemiologic category, race, calendar year, or national-estimate strata are encoded with role=exposure only to satisfy the schema context contract; this does not imply causality.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to describe trends in invasive MRSA incidence among children during 2005 through 2010.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: OBJECTIVE: To describe trends in the incidence of invasive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections in children during 2005–2010.

atoms.canonical_statement: ABCs conducted active, population-based surveillance for laboratory-confirmed invasive MRSA in selected counties across 9 metropolitan areas, covering about 4.4 million people younger than 18 years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The Active Bacterial Core Surveillance (ABCs) for invasive MRSA infections is an active, population-based surveillance system for laboratory-confirmed MRSA that started in July 2004 in selected counties in 9 geographically diverse metropolitan areas with a population of ~4.4 million persons younger than 18 years

population.label: ABCs surveillance population younger than 18 years

atoms.canonical_statement: An invasive MRSA case required MRSA isolation from a normally sterile body site in a surveillance-area resident younger than 18 years, at least 30 days after an initial invasive MRSA culture.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A case of invasive MRSA infection was defined by the isolation of MRSA from a normally sterile body site (eg, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, pleural fluid) in a surveillance area resident younger than 18 years at least 30 days apart of an initial invasive MRSA culture.

population.label: Surveillance-area residents younger than 18 years
inclusion_criteria: MRSA isolated from a normally sterile body site
At least 30 days apart from an initial invasive MRSA culture

atoms.canonical_statement: Surveillance staff abstracted demographic and clinical characteristics, outcomes, and established health care risk factors from medical records.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Surveillance personnel routinely receive all positive MRSA clinical microbiology reports from laboratories serving residents of surveillance areas. Demographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, disease outcomes, and information on established health care risk factors (ie, history of hospitalization [not including admission to a levelI, well-newborn nursery], surgery, dialysis, or residence in a long-term care facility in the previous year; or Author Manuscript presence of a central venous catheter within 2 days before culture) were abstracted from medical records.

atoms.canonical_statement: Hospital-onset cases were those with MRSA culture obtained on or after hospital day 4.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Cases were considered hospital- onset (HO) if the MRSA clinical culture was obtained on or after the fourth calendar day of hospitalization, where admission was hospital day 1;

atoms.canonical_statement: Health care-associated community-onset cases were outpatient or before hospital day 4 and had an established health care risk factor.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: as health care–associated community- onset (HACO) if the culture was obtained in an outpatient setting or before the fourth calendar day of hospitalization in a patient with an established health care risk factor;

atoms.canonical_statement: Community-associated cases were outpatient or before hospital day 4 without documentation of an established health care risk factor.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: and as CA if the culture was obtained in an outpatient setting or before the fourth calendar day of hospitalization in a patient without documentation of a health care risk factor.

atoms.canonical_statement: Among young infants, early-onset infection was defined as MRSA isolation before 3 days of age and late-onset infection as 3 through 89 days of age.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Among young infants, cases were categorized as early-onset infection if MRSA was isolated from infants younger than 3 days or late-onset infection if infants were 3 to 89 days of age.

atoms.canonical_statement: A convenience sample of MRSA isolates was sent to CDC for confirmation, susceptibility testing, and molecular characterization including PFGE.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: As part of surveillance, a convenience sample of MRSA isolates is sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for further testing as described elsewhere.6,12 Briefly, isolates undergo confirmation of S aureus identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and molecular characterization, including pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE).

atoms.canonical_statement: Beginning in 2008, submitted isolates were characterized by PFGE or by inference from microbiological characteristics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Beginning in 2008, all submitted isolates were characterized either by PFGE or by inference of PFGE patterns on the basis of microbiological characteristics, including staphylococcal cassette chromosome, presence of Panton-Valentine leukocidin, and antimicrobial susceptibility results.

atoms.canonical_statement: Incidence denominators used US Census bridged-race postcensus estimates, and race was imputed for cases with unknown race using known race and gender distributions within each surveillance area.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Incidence rates were calculated by using US Bureau of the Census bridged-race vintage postcensus population estimates.14–16 For cases in patients with unknown race, race was imputed on the basis of the distribution of known race and gender for each surveillance area.

atoms.canonical_statement: Because monthly infant population estimates were unavailable, the population younger than 90 days was approximated as one-quarter of the population younger than 1 year.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Because there are no population estimates for infants by month of age, we estimated that the population of infants younger than 90 days was approximately one-quarter of the population of infants younger than 1 year.

atoms.canonical_statement: Trend analyses were restricted to surveillance areas reporting continuously throughout the study period.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: To ensure comparability over time, analyses comparing incidence over time were restricted to surveillance areas that reported continuously during the study period.

atoms.canonical_statement: Incidence trends used Poisson regression or negative binomial regression when overdispersion was present, with models adjusted for age, gender, and race and statistical significance set at P less than .05.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Trends in incidence were assessed by using a Poisson regression model or negative binomial Author Manuscript distribution, if there was evidence of overdispersion. For cases in patients aged 3 to 89 days, annual incidences of all late-onset invasive MRSA infections and of HO infections were used to calculate trends. For cases in patients aged 90 days to 17 years, trends in incidences were calculated by epidemiologic category. The outcome variable was number of invasive MRSA infections, and time (year) as a continuous variable was the predictor. All models for trend analysis were adjusted by age, gender, and race; and P values <.05 were considered statistically significant.

atoms.canonical_statement: National 2010 case estimates applied age- and race-specific surveillance incidence to the US population, with confidence intervals estimated using a gamma-distribution method.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: For national estimates of cases in 2010, age- and race-specific incidence of infection across surveillance sites were applied to the age and racial distribution of the US population. CIs were estimated by using a method based on the gamma distribution.17

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Second, the sample of MRSA isolates received at the CDC was a sample of less than one-third of the pediatric cases reported and should not be interpreted as representative of all pediatric cases.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that invasive MRSA disproportionately affected young infants and black children, that health care-associated invasive MRSA did not significantly decline among children older than 3 months during 2005 through 2010, and that community-associated invasive MRSA incidence increased.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In summary, invasive MRSA infection in children appears to disproportionately affect young infants and black children. In contrast to declining incidence among adults and NICU patients, there were no significant reductions in invasive health care–associated MRSA infections in children older than 3 months during 2005–2010. Concurrently, the incidence of invasive CA-MRSA infections increased.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors interpreted the decline in late-onset invasive MRSA among hospitalized infants as likely due in part to NICU infection-prevention progress, but the surveillance study did not directly test that causal mechanism.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The observed decline is likely due in part to progress in infection prevention practices in NICUs, especially improvements in central line insertion and maintenance practices. This interpretation is supported by results of studies from NICU collaboratives that have implemented programs designed to improve central line practices leading to substantial reductions in central line– Author Manuscript associated BSIs (CLABSIs) caused by all pathogens.32–35
